claim: The tone controls these two types carry are one pair of first-order shelves whose corners are fixed and have no byte: a low shelf near 161 Hz and a high shelf near 6987 Hz, each of them a point inside a range these readings leave open rather than a number they resolve. The pair is the same pair on both types -- fitted to each type on its own the low corners land 0.0 octaves apart and the high ones 0.0119, and one shared pair scores each record as well as its own fit does. The section is one pole and one zero: a unit-slope second-order shelf is two to three times worse on the median of every one of the four records and three times worse at its worst, and its worst band is in the shelf's own transition every time. The gain is not fitted here at all -- it is the window the gain class closed on, twenty-five values centred on 64 that stick at both ends, and the same window that type 01 00 was read with. Six front halves carry one pair, and the corner is a range and not a number. Four further front halves were swept at the same two addresses, chosen for having nothing in common with the first two or with each other: 01 02 (a generator of harmonics with nothing summed in), 01 20 (eight all-pass sections turned down to the dry signal), 01 25 (an amplitude modulator at no depth), 02 06 (two blocks in series). The pair reproduces all four to a median of 0.160 dB or better against spans of twenty decibels and more, worst band 4.78 dB, and the second-order pair is beaten on every record the same way it was beaten before -- its best worst band anywhere in the six is 6.22 dB and it is inside the shelf's own transition every time. Three of the four carry no balance byte at all, so on those there is no direct half to park and what reached the gains is what the front half passed. **The corner is a range, and the round that closed this claim published it as a number.** Scanned over five octaves rather than refined around one grid point, every corner between 112 and 161 Hz fits the low shelf inside every record's own floor: those widths run to 1.55 octaves and the narrowest is 0.52. The high side has been read twice since -- once through a shelf whose half-gain point is where its parameter says it is, and once on a grid 25 times finer than the one that found it -- and it comes back 6872 to 7240 Hz, a band of 5.4 per cent shared by the five records whose own floors close on it. It is far narrower than it was and it is still a range. The two corners the model carries sit inside those ranges and are kept, because nothing measured moves them and a second point estimate would be the same artefact with a different value. What the agreement between types is worth is that no type's range sits outside the others' -- which is what was being asked, and is now asked of six.
named: a fixed first-order shelf pair, the part's tone control
adds: The records say what each gain byte did to each band at four settings of the low control and two of the high, on two types. What is read out of them here is that those profiles are shelves, that the shelves are one pole and one zero rather than a pair, where the corners are, and that the two types' corners are the same corners. The records name no filter, no corner and no order, and say so.
refutedBy: A tone control on a third type whose corners are not these, which would make the pair the type's rather than the part's. Or either shelf read with a band set reaching past where it settles and coming back at twelve decibels an octave.

eraPriors.claim: A tone control with no corner byte is a section written once with its coefficients compiled in, reached by whichever type wants one.
eraPriors.why: A corner nobody can set needs no table and no runtime arithmetic, so the cheap thing is one routine with two constants in it. Two types built at different times would have no reason to land on the same two constants.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: A third type's tone controls came back on a different pair of corners, which would make the pair the type's and not the part's.

alternatives.reading: A unit-slope second-order shelf, which is the shelf a part that already has biquads gets for free.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Its worst band is in the shelf's own transition on every record -- 6.2 to 6.6 decibels out where the first-order pair is 0.15 to 2.34 on the high side and 1.94 to 4.78 on the low -- and it has to move the corner to get there: fitted on its own it puts the low shelf at 291 Hz against 161 and the high at 3.1 kHz against 7.0, and is still several times as far out. A slope twice as steep cannot be hidden in a corner. The first-order figures here are what a shelf whose half-gain point is where its parameter says returns; read through the renderer as it was they were 2.0 to 2.4, and the second-order ones did not move at all, because the cookbook section next door was exact at every corner all along.

alternatives.reading: The pair is shared because the two types call one routine, rather than because two routines were given the same two constants.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: Not applicable: the two readings differ in where the code is and in nothing that comes out of it.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: The same shape recorded twice in the same archive. What the agreement does rule out is two *different* pairs, which is the thing that was worth asking: corners fitted to each type separately land 0.0 and 0.0119 octaves apart, under what either band set resolves.

On the low control the swing is between 25 Hz and 59 Hz, where this run's own repeats of one setting spread 0.31 and 1.11 decibels against 0.05 above 100 -- the signed median alternates sign across those bands rather than running one way. figures.why_the_count_and_not_the_verdict_moved: The reading under this gate was written when four records carried the claim and it is the reading the further eight return as well: the low control's swing sits in the bands below a hundred hertz where this stimulus has little energy, and the high control's where the deviation had not finished climbing when the band set ended. Neither is the model breaking down and both are bounds the records publish for themselves.

This claim's rule is an address, because the two gains it is about are the same two addresses on forty-two types. Type 11 08 is not one of them: it prints no tone control and puts one of its two halves' output levels at `40 03 13` instead. So the rule catches a record of a different parameter, and it is dropped here rather than the rule being narrowed to a list of types -- a list would be somebody choosing which readings the model is held against, which is the one thing generating the set is for. An address is a place and not a meaning, and this is the record that says so.

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// roland-sc8850-01  ·  filter-section
//
// Generated by yarn sync from inferences/models/tone-a-fixed-shelf-pair-order-1.json.
// The claim it closes: inferences/roland-sc8850-01/tone-a-pair-of-fixed-first-order-shelves.json
//
// Every constant, every section count and every structural choice below is
// the model's. The difference equations are the ordinary realisations of the
// sections the model names — this site's arithmetic, not a measurement.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#include <cmath>

namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::filter_section {

// Carried from the classes that measured it rather than fitted here. A shelf this far
// below half the rate is its analogue self whichever of the candidate rates is used, so
// this record cannot and need not say.
constexpr double kSampleRateHz = 32000.0;
constexpr double kPi = 3.14159265358979323846;

/**
 * A first-order shelf: one pole, one zero, tilting the two sides of its corner
 * against each other. `(s + w0 * V) / (s + w0)` for a low shelf and
 * `(V * s + w0) / (s + w0)` for a high one, bilinear-transformed.
 */
struct Shelf1 {
  enum class Side { Low, High };

  double b0 = 1.0, b1 = 0.0, a1 = 0.0, x1 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0;

  void set(double hz, double gainDb, Side side) {
    const double v = std::pow(10.0, gainDb / 20.0);
    const double k = std::tan(kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
    const double norm = 1.0 / (1.0 + k);
    a1 = (k - 1.0) * norm;
    if (side == Side::Low) {
      b0 = (1.0 + v * k) * norm;
      b1 = (v * k - 1.0) * norm;
    } else {
      b0 = (v + k) * norm;
      b1 = (k - v) * norm;
    }
  }

  double process(double x) {
    const double y = b0 * x + b1 * x1 - a1 * y1;
    x1 = x;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

// a ramp from -12 at 52 to 12 at 76, holding both ends
// read from data/units/roland-sc8850-01/efx-bands/01-00-04-how-much-is-twelve-db-fine-in-twelfths.json
inline double shelf0GainDb(int byte) {
  if (byte <= 52) return -12.0;
  if (byte >= 76) return 12.0;
  const double t = (byte - 52) / 24.0;
  return -12.0 + t * 24.0;
}

// a ramp from -12 at 52 to 12 at 76, holding both ends
// read from data/units/roland-sc8850-01/efx-bands/01-00-04-how-much-is-twelve-db-fine-in-twelfths.json
inline double shelf1GainDb(int byte) {
  if (byte <= 52) return -12.0;
  if (byte >= 76) return 12.0;
  const double t = (byte - 52) / 24.0;
  return -12.0 + t * 24.0;
}

/** The chain the model names, in the order it names it. */
struct Effect {
  Shelf1 shelf0;
  Shelf1 shelf1;

  void prepare(int b40_03_13, int b40_03_14) {
    shelf0.set(160.596898725, shelf0GainDb(b40_03_13), Shelf1::Side::Low);
    shelf1.set(6986.97926063, shelf1GainDb(b40_03_14), Shelf1::Side::High);
  }

  double process(double x) {
    x = shelf0.process(x);
    x = shelf1.process(x);
    return x;
  }
};
